work.title: Foster, You're Dead
work.first_publication: Star Science Fiction Stories No. 3, edited by Frederik Pohl, 1955

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: In a Cold War future organized entirely around the threat of imminent nuclear and bacterial attack, schoolboy Mike Foster is the only child in his class whose family has no private bomb shelter, because his father Bob, a struggling furniture-store owner, is a defiant 'anti-P' who refuses to buy into what he sees as a manufactured, endless arms-race consumer racket. Mike is tormented by his exposure — no permit for the school shelter, no vaccinations that will matter if he can't survive the blast itself — and haunted nightly by the gleaming, twenty-thousand-dollar shelters on display at the General Electronics showroom. Under pressure from his wife and son and his own guilt at having once challenged the President's shelter-economy directly, Bob finally buys a shelter on credit, and Mike experiences it as a kind of religious rapture, an enclosed, self-sufficient world where nothing is lacking and nothing can reach him. His happiness lasts only until a new Soviet weapon (bore-pellets, which burrow to seek warmth underground) renders the shelter's protection obsolete, forcing families to buy costly new 'adaptor' grills; unable to afford both the store and the upgrade before Christmas, Bob quietly returns the shelter for a partial refund, without telling his son until Mike discovers the empty pit himself. Mike disappears in shock and is later found, silent and catatonic, hiding inside the store's demonstration shelter after hours; dragged out by force, he wanders the streets in a daze and the story ends on a garish public-shelter sign advertising 'PEACE ON EARTH, GOOD WILL TO MEN' for fifty cents admission.

structure.form: short story in four movements: exposure and shame, the purchase and rapture, the loss, the aftermath
movements: School and street life establish Mike's terror at having no shelter, and his father's principled but costly refusal to buy one.
Bob relents; the shelter is purchased and installed, and Mike experiences it as an all-consuming private paradise.
A new Soviet weapon renders the shelter obsolete overnight; Bob, unable to afford the required upgrade, secretly returns it.
Mike's catatonic collapse, his discovery hiding in a demonstration shelter, and the story's closing image of a public shelter offering fifty-cent admission at Christmas.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Mike throughout, so the shelter economy's absurdities and cruelties are filtered entirely through a child's undiluted, literal terror rather than an adult's ironic distance.
structure.central_device: A domestic consumer purchase (a bomb shelter) treated with the emotional register of religious salvation, so that its repossession functions structurally as a loss of faith rather than a mere financial setback.

characters.name: Mike Foster
characters.note: His rapture inside the shelter and his catatonic collapse when it is repossessed are treated by the story with total narrative seriousness — this is a child's genuine religious experience and its genuine loss, not an exaggeration for satirical effect.

characters.name: Bob Foster
characters.note: Correctly diagnoses the entire shelter economy as an artificial, permanent arms-race protection racket — 'buy or die... the perfect sales-pitch' — and is nonetheless economically forced to participate in and then withdraw from it, proving his own analysis right at his own family's expense.

characters.name: Ruth Foster
characters.note: Pressures her husband to buy the shelter primarily out of social shame at being the town's last 'anti-P' family, a motive the story treats as understandable rather than shallow.

characters.name: Mrs. Cummings
characters.note: Administers the school's civil-defense curriculum (digging, trap-making, knife-sharpening) with weary institutional normalcy, and is genuinely startled to learn a student in her class has no shelter permit at all.

settings.name: The General Electronics showroom
settings.note: A shrine-like retail display for successive shelter models, its advertising copy ('e-z payment plan') rendering apocalypse preparation as a consumer product line indistinguishable from cars or television sets.

settings.name: The Foster family shelter
settings.note: Installed and then repossessed within a single school term, its brief existence giving Mike the only unconditional sense of safety and completeness he experiences in the story.

motifs: Apocalypse preparedness marketed and financed exactly like consumer durables — trade-ins, easy-payment plans, planned obsolescence, seasonal models
A father's political principle (refusing the shelter economy) proven correct by events and ruinous to his family regardless
A child's genuine rapture inside a purchased shelter, narrated with the seriousness of religious ecstasy rather than childish wonder
Escalating weapons technology used explicitly to force continuous new consumer purchases, stated outright by a character as 'the perfect sales-pitch'
A public shelter's Christmas admission fee closing the story on the same commodification of safety that opened it
reading.significance: Dick's own story note states his intent with striking directness: he was 'furious' at a real newspaper account of a presidential suggestion that citizens buy their own bomb shelters rather than have the government provide them, and wrote the story specifically 'to show how cruel the authorities can be when it comes to human life, how they can think in terms of dollars, not people.' The story's power comes from refusing every possible softening of that thesis — Bob Foster's political critique is not merely rhetorically correct, it is proven true by the plot itself, and this vindication brings his family no relief, only a second loss layered on top of the first. Mike's collapse is the story's real subject: a child's capacity for genuine faith and genuine devastation, exploited by a system that markets survival itself as a luxury good with planned obsolescence built in.
reading.closing_note: The story's final image — a garish 'PEACE ON EARTH, GOOD WILL TO MEN' sign advertising fifty-cent shelter admission — delivers its bitterest irony without any further narrative comment, leaving the juxtaposition to do all the work.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a permanent civil-defense arms-race economy that markets survival itself as a consumer product with engineered obsolescence
a child's genuine, unironized religious rapture inside a purchased shelter, and his genuine devastation at its loss
apocalypse preparedness rendered in the exact vocabulary and social pressure of ordinary suburban consumer purchases — trade-ins, keeping up with neighbors, seasonal models

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick's own story note states his exact motivating anger with unusual directness, naming a specific news story that provoked the piece.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: One day I saw a newspaper headline reporting that the President suggested that if Americans had to buy their bomb shelters, rather than being provided with them by the government, they'd take better care of them, an idea which made me furious. Logically, each of us should own a submarine, a jet fighter, and so forth. Here I just wanted to show how cruel the authorities can be when it comes to human life, how they can think in terms of dollars, not people. (1976)
evidence.reading: A direct, unusually specific statement of the story's origin and thesis — a genuine news item provoking genuine anger, channeled into fiction with almost no allegorical distance.

open_questions: Which specific presidential statement or news report is Dick recalling? Identifying the actual 1950s source would sharpen the story's historical grounding.

No secondary criticism was found for this story despite its clear thematic connections to Dick's other consumer-anxiety fiction (compare sales-pitch and nanny, both read in this project) — worth flagging as an archive gap for acquisition.

Mrs. Cummings' civil-defense curriculum (digging, trap-making) is presented with total institutional normalcy — is there a documented real-world basis in 1950s American civil-defense education Dick may have drawn on directly?
